Absolutely fascinating article, and speaking as someone who's only been in the workforce for the past decade and a half, I have to say I have seen the rise of many of these things.

I worked in call centers for a few years, but even as I was working there, there was a tension growing borne of two reasons. One, was automated calls for outgoing and ingoing calls were impacting the work we were capable of doing, and the arguable necessity of our labor. The other, was the rise of call centers in foreign countries that could operate at a fraction of the cost of ours, although that latter option was not good for the consumers or the workers, just the people at the top. This is a fairly literal way that technology was outsourcing our ability to do the jobs, and of the three call centers I worked for when I was younger, two are now gone.

My buddy has been working in a union doing construction projects for the past decade or so. He has also witnessed the rise of automation strangling jobs and lowering personnel needs, even in that short time frame. He's working on becoming a foreman so that he is more likely to still have job options by the time he's ready to retire, if he ever does, because they simply need less and less people as time progresses.

I have several friends who work as secretaries and paralegals in the legal field. Technology however, is increasingly making jobs like those irrelevant. There is less and less support staff needed every year, as fewer and fewer people are capable of handling more tasks thanks to computers and superior networks. For that matter, keeping paper records on file and in order is becoming obsolete as more databases are converted into data storage rather than hard copies. The younger attorneys don't really need a secretary at all it feels like, while the older attorneys are slowly retiring and leaving the work force, and leaving a sizable gap in the middle where lots of support staff are becoming increasingly obsolete.

As was pointed out in the article, driverless cars will dramatically impact the workforce if they're able to haul semis cross-country. Those are good, high paying, skilled jobs that are going to one day in the near future, totally fucking disappear.

Fast food workers, while in the process of pushing for a higher, livable wage, are shortly going to be replaced by automation. Can you imagine, soon there will be fast food chains that don't actually need a human at to operate. Driverless trucks to deliver the goods, automated machines to dispatch and store, assembly line efficiency at crafting the requested orders, and an automated machine to take the order itself. The only humans needed would be the customers--that's a day that's on the horizon.

I think the article is right on the money in pointing these things out as being something we need to concern ourselves with immediately. This is something that globally, we need to start talking about. The problems that the article described are absolutely something that we will face in our generation, and they're unprecedented in the entirety of human existence.
